title: How match-fixing shows itself
body_html:
HOW MATCH-FIXING SHOWS ITSELF

The expected result of a sports competition depends either on the player taking part in it directly or on the referee (refereeing panel) whose duties include applying the rules of the game being played. These two groups can be described as having direct influence on the outcome of the competition (direct participants).

However, the result of a sporting event may also be manipulated by a third party, such as the representative or owner of a sports club, who is able to influence the environment in which the event takes place. These individuals can be described as having indirect influence on the outcome of the match (indirect participants).

In sports such as table tennis, padel or tennis, in a one-on-one format where both players are involved in fixing the game, the agreement usually consists of choosing in advance the winner of the match or of its intermediate stages (for example, one of the games).

Another common form of arrangement is when one player is allowed to progress through a tournament to improve their overall standing, while their opponent takes prize money as compensation for accepting defeat.

And the most common form of manipulation is when a player deliberately loses a match or intermediate stages without the opponent knowing about it (including deliberately withdrawing from the competition for reasons unrelated to sport).

In team sports such as football, a typical form of collusion is a prior agreement between teams or groups of players from each team. As a rule, this form of match-fixing involves agreeing that a particular team will win the match, at a specific moment and with an agreed number of goals scored. If only one team, or a group of members of one team, is involved in the collusion, this usually means deliberately losing the match or an intermediate stage of it and/or manipulating the final score.

Fixed or rigged matches can also be organised by referees and other competition officials. In football, for example, there are a number of ways in which a referee can fraudulently influence the result of a match or any of its components, such as the number of goals scored.

Manipulating a match can also involve influencing the result through other elements of the sporting event, such as interfering with the equipment or with the process on the court/playing area where the competition takes place.

A tournament’s structure can also compromise the integrity of sport and give match-fixers substantial opportunities to make money in betting markets. The most common form of match-fixing of this kind involves participants in a match, or a team taking part in a competition, agreeing the result of a match in order to influence the performance of the opponent they will face in the next match.

So how are fixed matches detected, and why is it easier to “recruit” a participant in table tennis or tennis events than, for example, in a team sport like football?

First, there are hundreds of routine table tennis matches that people bet on, and these are matches in which nothing out of the ordinary should happen. If the betting on one of them is abnormally high and on just one outcome, that match will at least be placed in the category of suspicious events.

Reasonable suspicion grows as investigations progress, and factors pointing to a fixed sporting event include, in particular, the characteristics of the bettor: a recently created account; little or no betting history on the platform or on this sport; personal details and betting location that fully or partly coincide with the location of the event or have some link to one of its participants; an unusually large bet on a high-odds outcome (above 3); an unusually high percentage of winning bets from the same account; an account active only for the events of one and the same participant; a participant’s limited playing history and experience, and so on.

Second, what makes table tennis more attractive to fraudsters is the individual nature of the sport and each player’s independence in making decisions, regardless of the wishes and intentions of the coach or tournament organiser, clubmates or referees. It is easier to strike a deal with one greedy, unprincipled, narrow-minded and petty player than with a whole team, as in football or basketball.

The variety of events offers many opportunities for manipulation, since the favourite does not have to lose the match at all. It is enough to lose one game, naively believing the act will stay beyond suspicion. In fact, that is not the case at all, and the bitter experience of the last two years in Moldovan table tennis has proved it conclusively.
